doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Hearing their arrangements played: Clyde Reisinger and the radio
summary: The thrill of Clyde Reisinger's big band recording 'Homeward Bound', and hearing the Sweet Baby Blues Band on radio.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well can you tell me about the first time that you heard one of your own arrangements played that really gave you a thrill?
Yeah.
It was Clyde Reisinger for me. When they did—
Yeah. That was really one of the thrills because we weren’t in Buffalo then.
No. We were in New York City.
With who now?
Clyde Reisinger.
His big band.

He used to be a great lead player, and he lived in Hollywood, in Los Angeles too, and so he worked the studio and did a lot of lead playing and stuff like that. And then he went to New York and that’s when we saw him again.
We rehearsed with the big band.
We rehearsed with the big band and we recorded with him. Those dates were set up, where we featured him. That was on “Homeward Bound.”
“Homeward Bound.” One of the tunes we wrote.
And he just loved that, and he had never had anybody write a feature for him, and set him up. He said at the time he considered it the best ballads that he’s ever enjoyed performing.
A great arranger. Who had the arrangements done? I want to talk about him. Because he was supposed to send it back so we could get copies of it.
Wasn’t that the drummer that has the band?
You probably interviewed him anyway.
Right now I can’t think of it. I’m looking at his face.
And then when we heard ourselves on radio for the first time with the Sweet Baby Blues Band.
Yeah, that was the other thrill. On record.
It was really startling, to say the least. That really was a thrill.
It was mind blowing. Just in a sense because, I’m trying to recall when I wrote this or wrote that. And it was kind of hard to record.
It sounded like somebody else.

Yeah. Because like I said, you know, because I did a lot, in fact both of us did a lot with our intuitivity, you know, our intuitiveness you see. And so you give those things, and it’s not only in the writing but also solo-wise. So to recall what you played, is very
difficult for either one of us. And then when we hear it back, it sounded like somebody else was playing. And then you realize that it’s not anybody else, because —
Was I really on this?
Yeah. Where was I when this was happening?
